item.title: Agentic AI with LangChain — Part 7: Building Multi-Agent Systems with LangGraph
item.content:encoded:
Multi-agents systems are becoming a foundational pattern in agentic AI. As workflows grow more complex, including retrieval, tool use, planning, and delegation, single-agent architectures begin to show structural weaknesses. This seventh installment of the Agentic AI with LangChain series introduces multi-agent architectures in LangGraph, demonstrating how specialization, modularity, and peresistent state significantly improve reliability and scalability.

Up to now, our workflows relied on LangGraph StateGraphs to maintain execution state and a single LLM agent to plan actions, select tools, invoke them, and process tool messages. Through iterative tool calls, this agent produced final results using the ReAct pattern described in Part 4 and Part 5 of the series.

While effective for small systems, single-agent designs introduce four structural limitations:

  • State lifespan: State exists only during graph execution. Once the graph completes, all state is lost.
  • Tool overload: One agent sees every tool. As the toolset grows, the agent’s context window becomes saturated with tool prompts, tool messages, and instructions.
  • Attention competition: Prompts compete for focus, increasing the likelihood of missed instructions or incorrect tool selection.
  • Tool routing difficulty: As more tools accumulate, selecting the correct tool becomes increasingly unreliable.

To address these issues, we introduce multi-agent workflows using LangGraph. We begin by adding an InMemorySaver checkpointer to persist messages across conversations. Next, we decompose the workflow into subagents, each responsible for a specific task and exposed only to the tools relevant to that task. This reduces context-window pressure, improves routing reliability, and makes the system easier to maintain.

Why Multi-Agents Matter

Multi-agent systems embody a core principle of scalable AI engineering: task decomposition. Instead of one agent managing everything, we break a complex workflow into smaller subtasks handled by specialized subagents. Each subagent has its own system prompt, tool list and focused responsibility. This specialization sacrifices some flexibility but significantly improves reliability, maintainability, and production-grade behavior.

🧰Technical Concepts Used in This Article

Before diving into the multi-agents architectures, it is helpful to clarify several core LangGraph concepts that appear throughout this article. These concepts form the foundation of how multi-agent workflows maintain state, coordinate tasks, and manage conversations. They also lay the groundwork for our next article on the deep agents.

Task decomposition

Breaking a complex workflow into smaller, specialized subtasks. Each subtask is handled by a dedicated subagent with its own system prompt and tool list. This improves reliability, reduces context-window pressure, and makes the workflow easier to maintain.

Messages

Messages represent the conversation history, including user messages, AI messages, and tool messages. Multi-agent systems rely on message passing to coordinate work among subagents and maintain continuity across tool calls.

Threads

A thread is an identifier for a single ongoing conversation. If multiple calls share the same thread_id, LangGraph treats them as part of the same session. This allows agents to remember previous turns and maintain continuity across separate invocations.

Checkpointer

A checkpointer stores thread state between calls. It ensures that multi-turn workflows remain reliable by saving the current thread and restoring it when the next call uses the same thread_id. In this article, we use InMemorySaver as the simplest checkpointer for local development.

Project Overview: A Financial Assistant Agent

To demonstrate multi-agent systems, we build a financial assistant agent capable of researching Fortune 500 companies and analyzing their stock performance using three tools:

  • Wikipedia tool: retrieves company summaries
  • Stock data tool: fetches stock price data from Yahoo Finance
  • Python REPL tool: generates stock performance visualizations

We implement this assistant using two multi-agent patterns in LangGraph:

  • Swarm multi-agents
  • Supervisor multi-agents

Both implementations use an InMemorySaver checkpointer as the persistent layer.

The complete code for this article is available in the GitHub Repo.

1. System Configuration

Create a .env file in the project root and define all required API keys:

OPENAI_API_KEY="<Your OpenAI API Key>"
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT="https://api.smith.langchain.com"
LANGSMITH_API_KEY="<Your LangSmith API Key"
LANGSMITH_PROJECT="agent-ai"

Load these variables using a Pydantic BaseSettings class:

class BaseConfig(BaseSettings):
    OPENAI_API_KEY: Optional[str]    

model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore")

2. Project Structure

Full code available in GitHub Repo

project/
├── tools/       
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── financial_search.py # fetch stock prices for companies
│   ├── python_REPL.py      # async wrapper of PythonREPL()
|   └── wikipedia_search.py # fetch financial summary of companies
│   
├── graphs/            # implement subagents and multi-agents
│   ├── agent.py       # implement research and analyst in a single agent
│   ├── sub_agents.py  # implement research and analyst sub agents
│   ├── multi_agent_supervisor.py # implement supervisor multi-agents
│   └── multi_agent_swarm.py # implement swamp multi-agents
│
├── config.py           # pydantic BaseConfig
│── utils.py            # utility for printing and executing agents
├── .env                # environment variable definition     
├── .gitignore
└── requirements.txt     # package requirements

3. Tools of the Financial Assistant Agent

Below are selected code blocks that illustrate the core tools used by the agent. Full implementations are available in the GitHub Repo.

3.1. Stock Data Search Tool

Code in tools/financial_search.py

This tool wraps Yahoo Finance’s API and returns a formatted DataFrame.

# define LangChain tool to retrieve stock data 
@tool
async def stock_data_tool(
        company_ticker: Annotated[str, "The ticker symbol of the company to retrieve their stock performance data."],
        num_days: Annotated[int, "The number of business days of stock data required to respond to the user query."]
) -> str:
    
        # fetch stock data asynchronously from yfinance
        # check full code for _fetch_stock_sync function
        df = await asyncio.to_thread(_fetch_stock_sync, company_ticker, f"{num_days}d")
        
        return (f"Successfully executed the stock performance data retrieval tool to retrieve "
                f"the last *{num_days} days* of data for company **{company_ticker}**:

{df.to_markdown()}")

3.2. Python Code Execution Tool

Code in tools/python_REPL.py

This tool executes Python code using PythonREPL and is used to generate stock performance plots.

@tool
async def python_repl_tool(
        code: Annotated[str, "The python code to execute to generate your chart."],
) -> str: 

    # wrap LLM generated code and execute it by python.REPL()
    # repl = PythonREPL().  
    clean_code = textwrap.dedent(code).strip()
    result = await asyncio.to_thread(repl.run, clean_code)
    
    return (
        f"Successfully executed the Python REPL tool.

"
        f"Python code executed:
```python
{code}
```

"
        f"Code output:
```
{result}```"
    )

3.3. Wikipedia Search Tool

Code in tools/wikipedia_search.py

This tool performs asynchronous Wikipedia searches using httpx

@tool()
async def wikipedia_tool(
        query: Annotated[str, "The Wikipedia search to execute to find key summary information."],
) -> str:
    """Use this to search Wikipedia for factual information asynchronously."""
    headers = {"User-Agent": "MyLangChainAgent/1.0 (contact@example.com)"}

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(headers=headers, follow_redirects=True) as client:
        
        # Step 1: Search Wikipedia for matching pages
        search_url = "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php"
        search_params = {
            "action": "query",
            "list": "search",
            "srsearch": query,
            "format": "json"
        }
        response = await client.get(search_url, params=search_params)
        search_data = response.json()
        results = search_data.get("query", {}).get("search", [])   
        title = results[0]["title"]

        # Step 2: Fetch the page extract/summary
        summary_url = f"https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/summary/{title}"
        summary_res = await client.get(summary_url)
        summary_data = summary_res.json()
        summary = summary_data.get("extract", "No summary available.")

        return f"Successfully executed:
Wikipedia summary: {summary}"

4. Swarm Multi-Agents

4.1. Architecture of Swarm Multi-Agents

Swarm multi-agents consists of two specialized agents:

  • Research Agent: retrives company summaries and stock data
  • Analyst Agent: generates stock performance visualizations

Agents hand off tasks using create_handoff_tool from LangGraph. In addition, a start agent (Research Agent in this project) must be defined so the workflow knows where to begin.

Swarm multi-agents reduces tool overload and attention competition but introduces two challenges:

  • Infinite handoff loop: an agent hand offs a task to other agents if it can’t process that task. If no agents can process a task, then infinite handoff loops are created.
  • Start-agent ambiguity: swarm multi-agents requires explicit definition of the start agent, which some times is not straightforward and introduces challenges and redundancy.

4.2. Swarm Multi-agents Implementation

Full implementation available in graphs/multi-agent_swap.py

Selected code excerpts:

llm = ChatOpenAI(api_key=api_key, model="gpt-4o-mini")

# Create a handoff tool for researcher -> analyst
transfer_to_analyst = create_handoff_tool(
    agent_name="analyst",
    description="Transfer user to the analyst assistant, who can create visualizations of provided data.",
)

# create research agent as a subagent
research_agent = create_agent(
    llm,
    tools=[wikipedia_tool, stock_data_tool, transfer_to_analyst],
    system_prompt="You provide summaries from Wikipedia, and can query load raw, numerical stock performance data.",
    name="researcher"
)

# define the checkpointer
checkpointer = InMemorySaver()

# create swarm agents
swarm_agent = create_swarm(
    agents=[research_agent, analyst_agent],
    default_active_agent="researcher"
).compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

5. Supervisor Multi-Agents

5.1. Architecture of Supervisor Multi-Agents

Supervisor multi-agents solves swarm multi-agents limitations by introducing a supervisor agent to coordinate sub-agents. The supervisor receives user inputs, delegates tasks to subagents, processes results fetched from sub-agents and returns the final answer to users.

Supervisor agents eliminate infinite handoff loops with and improve reliability. However, they require more message passing because subagents do not communicate directly.

5.2. Supervisor Multi-agents Implementation

Full code available in graphs/multi-agent_supervisor.py

Selected code excerpts:

llm = ChatOpenAI(api_key=api_key, model="gpt-4o-mini")

# create a checkpointer
checkpointer = InMemorySaver()

# create research subagent
research_agent = create_agent(
    llm,
    tools=[wikipedia_tool, stock_data_tool],
    system_prompt="You provide summaries from Wikipedia, and can query load raw, numerical stock performance data.",
    name="researcher"
)

# Create the supervisor multi-agent graph and compile it
supervisor = create_supervisor(
    model=llm,
    agents=[research_agent, analyst_agent],
    prompt=(
        "You are a supervisor managing two agents:
"
        "- a research agent. Assign research and data collection tasks to this agent
"
        "- an analyst agent. Assign the creation of visualizations via code to this agent
"
        "Assign work to one agent at a time, do not call agents in parallel.
"
        "Do not do any work yourself."
    ),
    add_handoff_back_messages=True,
    output_mode="last_message"
).compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

6. Closing Summary

In this article, we implemented two multi-agent patterns: swarm and supervisor, and demonstrated how multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks into subtasks handled by specialized subagents. This reduces tool overload, simplifies prompts, improves routing reliability and mitigates attention competition.

However, multi-agent systems also have limitations:

  • Lack of file and data access control: Python REPL tool has full filesystem access. This is not encouraged, especially in a prod system
  • Lack of context-window management: subagent may still overload their context-windows during long workflows
  • Lack of subagent discovery: subagents must be explicitly defined, which limits scalability

These challenges motivate the next article in the series, where we introduce the deep agents in LangGraph, a design that addresses several limitations inherent to multi-agent systems.

Agentic AI with LangChain — Part 7: Building Multi-Agent Systems with LangGraph was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: MCP tool design: why your agent keeps calling the wrong tool
item.content:encoded:
An agent with both get_customer_by_id and get_customer_context on its tool list will, sooner or later, call the first one when the task actually needed the second. Nothing is broken. The model read two schemas that describe overlapping territory and made a reasonable guess, and the guess was wrong [1].

That single failure mode, not model capability, is behind most of the “my agent picked the wrong tool” reports that show up once a project grows past four or five tools. The fix rarely lives in the system prompt. It lives in the tool schema itself: the name, the description, and how many near-duplicate tools are sitting next to each other on the list Claude sees before it ever writes a line of reasoning.

In this article:

  • Why routing failures are a schema problem, not a prompting problem
  • What separates a tool description Claude reads correctly from one it doesn’t
  • Why consolidating tools beats writing better disambiguation text
  • How namespacing and MCP’s own schema fields cut down the guessing
  • A short audit to run before shipping a new tool surface

Routing failures are a schema problem, not a prompting problem

Claude picks a tool by reading its name, its description, and its parameter schema, then matching that text against the current task. There's no separate routing model doing lookup behind the scenes. The description string is the entire interface the model has to reason about intent, scope, and limits, which is why Claude's own documentation calls detailed tool descriptions "by far the most important factor in tool performance" [1].

That single sentence reframes the debugging problem. When an agent calls the wrong tool, the instinct is to add a clarifying line to the system prompt telling it when to use which tool. That patches one symptom without touching the cause: two tools whose descriptions overlap will keep colliding no matter what the surrounding prompt says, because the ambiguity lives in the part of the context the model consults first.

What separates a description Claude reads correctly from one it doesn’t

Anthropic’s tool-use documentation is specific about what a working description contains: what the tool does, when it should and shouldn’t be used, what each parameter means, and any caveats about what the tool does not return, aiming for at least three to four sentences per tool [1]. A one-line description leaves all of that unstated, and an unstated boundary is exactly where two tools start to overlap in the model’s read of them.

The get_stock_price example in that documentation makes the gap concrete. The poor version says the tool “gets the stock price for a ticker” and leaves the ticker parameter with no description at all. The effective version states the exchange constraint, the currency the result comes back in, and explicitly says what the tool won’t return [1]. Nothing about the underlying function changed. Only the text Claude reads before deciding whether to call it did.

This is also the exact failure mode covered by the MCP tool-design content inside Anthropic’s own certification tracks, where tool schemas, routing, and MCP server and client design form a dedicated exam domain rather than a footnote inside a broader integration topic, per the program’s official overview [4]. An independent study guide for that certification puts Tool Design & MCP Integration at 18% of the Architect Foundations exam, and a separate independent guide puts the developer-track Tools and MCPs domain at 10.6%, split roughly across tool implementation, MCP server development, and choosing between built-in tools, custom tools, and MCP servers [5][6]. Both figures come from third-party study resources rather than Anthropic’s own exam guide PDF, which wasn’t independently re-verifiable through this piece’s research, so treat the domain’s existence as confirmed and the exact percentages as reported by outside sources rather than Anthropic itself.

Consolidation beats writing better disambiguation text

Before reaching for a longer description, it’s worth asking whether the tool should exist as a separate entry at all. Anthropic’s engineering team makes the same point from the other direction: “more tools don’t always lead to better outcomes,” and an agent facing too many overlapping tools gets distracted from pursuing an efficient strategy rather than helped by the extra options [2].

Their recommended fix is consolidation rather than clarification. Instead of shipping list_users, list_events, and create_event as three separate tools competing for the same intent, group them behind a single schedule_event tool with an explicit action parameter [2]. The same pattern applies to a customer-support agent: rather than separate tools for get_customer_by_id, list_transactions, and list_notes, a single get_customer_context tool returns everything relevant to a customer in one call [2]. Fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity because there's less for the model to choose between at the moment it decides which tool to reach for [2].

Tool calling itself is the mechanism underneath all of this, the same structured-calling foundation covered in an earlier piece on the OpenAI function calling feature: a model reasons over a list of available functions and their schemas, then emits a structured call rather than free text. Consolidation doesn’t change that mechanism. It just shrinks the list the model has to reason over before making the call.

Namespacing and the parts of MCP’s schema that descriptions don’t cover

Once a project connects to more than one MCP server, tool names collide across services in a way a single well-written description can’t fix on its own. Anthropic’s guidance is to prefix tool names by service and, where useful, by resource: asana_search and jira_search rather than two tools both named search, or asana_projects_search and asana_users_search when a single service exposes multiple resource types [2]. The MCP specification backs this with hard constraints on the name field itself: tool names should stay between 1 and 128 characters, use only letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, and dots, and be unique within a server, so the naming convention that disambiguates for the model also has to fit the protocol's own rules [3].

MCP’s schema also carries fields a hand-rolled tool definition sometimes skips. Beyond name and description, a tool can declare a title field as a separate human-readable display label, and an optional annotations object describing behavior like whether a call is read-only or destructive [3]. That second field comes with a specific warning worth internalizing: clients must treat annotations as untrusted unless they come from a server the client already trusts, since a malicious or careless server can attach annotations that don't match what the tool actually does [3]. In practice, that means the description string, not the annotation metadata, remains the part of the schema doing the real disambiguation work, the same principle covered in more general terms in an earlier post on prompt engineering best practices around not letting metadata substitute for explicit, load-bearing text.

A short audit before shipping a new tool surface

Four checks catch most of this before a tool surface ships. First, read every tool description next to the others it will sit alongside and ask whether a reader with no other context could tell them apart in one pass. Second, look for any tool whose name differs from a neighbor only by a suffix like _by_id versus _context, since that naming pattern is itself a signal that the two should probably be one tool with a parameter. Third, check that every tool description states what the tool does not do or does not return, not just what it does, since the unstated boundary is where overlap hides. Fourth, if the project spans more than one external service, confirm every tool name carries a service prefix before it ships, rather than adding the prefix later once two tools have already collided in production.

None of these checks require a bigger model or a more clever prompt. They require treating the tool list itself as the thing under review, since that’s the text actually deciding which function runs.

Sources

  1. Define tools, Claude Platform Docs
  2. Writing effective tools for AI agents, Anthropic Engineering
  3. Tools, Model Context Protocol Specification
  4. Claude Certified Architect, Foundations, Anthropic Academy
  5. Claude Certified Architect (Foundations): Exam Guide and Blueprint, Claude Certification Guide (independent, unofficial)
  6. Tools and MCPs: Claude Certified Developer, Foundations Exam Prep, AI Skill Certs (independent, unofficial)

item.title: I Audited 4,523 AI Judgments. Here’s What I’d Check Before Trusting an Agent Team.
item.content:encoded:
Across 377 assets, a simple vote and a risk-aware scoring system disagreed in 45% of decisive cases. An audit you can borrow before your agents act.

Twelve AI agents. Twelve STRONG BUY ratings. What would you put on the screen?

Probably STRONG BUY. Perhaps a reassuring little badge: 100% agreement.

Now the awkward part. Three assets in our research snapshot had that identical ballot. Two finished STRONG BUY. The third finished BUY.

Same votes. Different verdict. So what was the vote not telling us?

Accenture and Adyen kept the stronger rating. The Trade Desk did not. Its agents hadn’t secretly changed their minds. Our scoring layer used information their labels could not carry: forecast magnitude, consistency, and risk.

That is the part I want anyone building an agent team to notice. You can collect every answer, count every vote correctly, and still throw away information that changes the decision.

The counting can be flawless. The summary can still be inadequate.

Think of twelve engineers saying a migration is ‘safe.’ One means a brief outage. Another means no outage but a painful rollback. A green badge makes them look unanimous. Ask what they mean by safe, and suddenly you have a meeting worth having.

I wanted to put a number on that gap.

We audited 4,523 agent judgments across 377 assets. In the 365 cases with a clear winning direction, a simple vote and the richer scoring system disagreed 166 times: about 45%.

No, that does not mean 45% of the forecasts were wrong. We compared two ways of summarizing model outputs, not predictions against future market results. But it does mean the choice of aggregator was consequential.

Before you pay for another agent, inspect what happens to the answers you already have. Here is the audit I would start with.

In an earlier investor-facing analysis, I examined how often these forecasts disagreed. Here, I reuse that snapshot to test a different engineering question: can the votes reproduce the final decision?

The snapshot comes from iPulse AI, the investment-research platform I build. Its live rankings can change; this audit uses the fixed July snapshot described below.

What you can steal from this audit

  • A baseline vote you can reproduce without another model call.
  • A transition matrix showing exactly where your aggregator changes the answer.
  • An identical-ballot test that exposes information your labels cannot preserve.
  • A way to separate agreement, disagreement, and actual confidence.
  • A decision record that lets you investigate a result instead of arguing with a screenshot.

First, count something embarrassingly simple

Our sample covered stocks, cryptoassets, commodities, indices, and currencies at a five-year forecast horizon. There were 376 assets with twelve analytical voices and one with eleven: 4,523 judgments in total. Each voice returned one of five ordered ratings, from strongly positive to strongly negative:

STRONG_BUY, BUY, NEUTRAL, PARTIALLY_SELL, SELL_ALL

For the baseline, I grouped STRONG_BUY and BUY as positive, kept NEUTRAL separate, and grouped PARTIALLY_SELL and SELL_ALL as negative. Whichever group had the most votes won:

positive = strong_buy + buy
negative = partially_sell + sell_all
if positive > max(neutral, negative):
    vote_direction = "POSITIVE"
elif negative > max(neutral, positive):
    vote_direction = "NEGATIVE"
elif neutral > max(positive, negative):
    vote_direction = "NEUTRAL"
else:
    vote_direction = "TIE"

Technically, this is a plurality, not necessarily a majority. Five positive, four neutral, and three negative votes produce a positive winner, although seven agents did not vote positive. A tied maximum stays a tie. That distinction already makes a ‘consensus’ badge less comforting.

The production aggregator had a different job. It retained continuous forecasts, volatility, directional consistency, dividend effects, and configured thresholds. I mapped its final ratings into the same three directions so the two methods could be compared.

The question was deliberately narrow: could the ballot reproduce the richer decision?

The answer was no. The interesting part was where it failed.

166 disagreements. Almost none were reversals.

Of 377 assets, twelve had a tied baseline vote. That left 365 decisive comparisons. In 166, the final direction differed. Here is what that 45% actually contained:

Read the destinations, not just the headline:

  • 98 positive pluralities became neutral.
  • 67 negative pluralities became neutral.
  • One negative plurality became positive.
  • No positive plurality became negative.

So 165 of the 166 disagreements ended at neutral. This was mostly a directional vote meeting a scoring threshold it did not clear, not a system shouting BUY while another shouted SELL.

Important distinction: NEUTRAL is a completed financial rating. ABSTAIN means the system declines to produce a decision. These records show the former; they do not prove the latter. Nor does landing at neutral prove the threshold was correct.

Still, imagine replacing that scoring layer with ‘most votes wins.’ You would be changing the decision policy while calling it a simpler implementation. That’s quite a refactor.

Then I tried saving every vote. Still not enough.

Maybe I had created the problem by squeezing five ratings into three directions. Fair objection. So I checked the full five-category ballot.

It still could not reconstruct the final label.

The 377 assets contained 267 distinct vote patterns. Twenty-four patterns appeared alongside more than one final rating. Those patterns covered 77 assets, about 20% of the sample.

The unanimous cases from the opening make this easy to see:

The Trade Desk had the highest annualized mean forecast of these three and the strongest direction-consistency reading. It also had the highest risk pressure, the lowest continuous consensus score, and the weaker final label. Those are model outputs, not realized returns or investment recommendations.

Think of star ratings. Two hotels can both score four stars while differing wildly on price, noise, and accessibility. Counting twelve four-star reviews does not recover the details that matter to your trip. A forecast label makes the same kind of compression.

Counting the labels compresses the evidence a second time.

My practical test: group records by the complete vote pattern, then count distinct final verdicts within each group. If a group has several verdicts, your ballot is missing inputs needed to explain them. That can be intentional and sensible. It must not be invisible.

Please stop turning agreement into a probability

Eight of twelve agents choose BUY. Agreement: 67%. Probability of being right: we have not established one. Changing the field name to ‘confidence’ does not finish the experiment.

Now compare eight BUY plus four STRONG BUY with eight BUY plus four SELL ALL. Same winning share. Very different opposition. One group argues about enthusiasm; the other argues about direction.

We measured categorical spread using normalized Shannon entropy. It describes how votes distribute across the five categories. Crucially, it cannot distinguish those two eight-to-four ballots either: the category proportions are identical. You still need the labels and their meaning. For proportions p_i across K categories:

H_norm = -sum(p_i * ln(p_i)) / ln(K)
from math import log
def normalized_vote_entropy(counts):
    if len(counts) != 5:
        raise ValueError('Expected all five rating counts')
    if any(type(c) is not int or c < 0 for c in counts):
        raise ValueError('Counts must be nonnegative integers')
    total = sum(counts)
    if total == 0:
        raise ValueError('No votes; do not invent agreement')
    probabilities = [c / total for c in counts if c]
    return -sum(p * log(p) for p in probabilities) / log(5)

Unanimity gives zero entropy. A more evenly spread ballot gives a higher value. Neither tells you whether the answer is correct. The denominator stays at five even when some categories have no votes.

Across our sample, however, higher entropy travelled with a noticeably different decision state:

In the lowest-entropy quarter, 5% of assets finished neutral. In the highest, 83% did. Average annual-return dispersion widened from roughly four percentage points to eight. Direction consistency fell from 0.84 to 0.71; risk pressure rose from 40 to 58.

These are associations inside one scoring system, not proof that entropy caused neutrality. My takeaway is simpler: keep uncertainty visible. One cheerful percentage is doing too many jobs.

What I’d change before adding agent thirteen

I would start with the handoff between agents and the application. The architecture diagram above shows the proposed flow. These five changes make that handoff inspectable; they are design recommendations, not claims that every feature was tested in this audit.

1. Keep the receipt, not just the verdict

Store each agent’s estimate, units, horizon, evidence timestamp, model version, and source references. This illustrative record is a starting point, not a production row:

{
  "agent_id": "value_v3",
  "rating": "BUY",
  "estimate": 0.14,
  "estimate_unit": "annualized_total_return_fraction",
  "horizon": "5Y",
  "evidence_as_of": "<timestamp>",
  "model_version": "<version>",
  "source_ids": ["<source-reference>"]
}

Otherwise, six months later you will know that an agent said BUY, but not what it was buying into. A string is cheap to store. An explanation is expensive to reconstruct.

2. Separate the questions your confidence badge hides

Keep distinct fields for:

  • Vote concentration: how tightly do the categories cluster?
  • Forecast dispersion: how far apart are the numerical estimates?
  • Directional consistency: do the modeled paths point the same way?
  • Dependence: how much model or source material is shared?
  • Freshness: what evidence is stale, absent, or incompatible?
  • Action cost: what happens if this decision is wrong?

Twelve personas using the same model and sources are not automatically twelve independent experts. Agent count tells you how many outputs arrived, not how many independent checks occurred. Separately, Google Research’s study of 180 agent configurations found that performance depended on architecture and task structure. Headcount alone is a poor design brief.

3. Make the decision policy something you can replay

Where comparable numerical estimates exist, test aggregating them before applying category thresholds. Keep risk rules explicit. Do not average incompatible horizons or units and hope that a persuasive summary will rescue the result.

Version the thresholds alongside the inputs. Otherwise, ‘the model changed its mind’ might really mean ‘we moved a boundary.’ Those deserve different investigations.

4. Give ‘not enough evidence’ its own exit

A system should be able to ask for missing evidence, route a case to a human, or abstain. A neutral rating cannot substitute for that branch: ‘I evaluated this and got neutral’ differs from ‘I could not evaluate this reliably.’

Specify the exit conditions before the result reaches an action button. Selective-classification research provides the useful framing: evaluate both the error on answered cases and how many cases the system answers.

5. Return a decision record you can investigate

For example, an illustrative abstention record could separate the process outcome from the domain rating:

{
  "decision_id": "<stable-id>",
  "decision_type": "ABSTAIN",
  "rating": null,
  "reasons": ["MISSING_REQUIRED_EVIDENCE"],
  "agent_records_ref": "<immutable-record-set>",
  "aggregation_version": "<version>",
  "decided_at": "<timestamp>"
}

The referenced record set should retain votes, continuous estimates, disagreement measures, and provenance. When the rating is completed, use a different decision type and populate it. Do not send both a normal rating and an unexplained abstention flag to a consumer and let it guess.

Fine. But does any of this make the answers better?

That is the question an enthusiastic architecture diagram cannot answer. More fields make investigation possible. They do not automatically make a forecast more accurate.

The next test has to use outcomes unavailable at decision time:

  1. Freeze agent outputs, evidence timestamps, and model and policy versions.
  2. Replay simple voting and richer aggregation on the same eligible cases.
  3. Measure directional and numerical forecast errors separately.
  4. For abstaining variants, report error alongside coverage: the proportion of cases answered.
  5. Check sensitivity to prompt, retrieval, model, and threshold changes.
  6. Include latency and cost. A better result can still be unusable if it arrives too late.

A system that answers one easy question and refuses the next ninety-nine can advertise beautiful accuracy. You probably would not hire it. That is why coverage belongs beside the score, not buried in a footnote.

Run the candidate in shadow mode first: record its proposed decisions without letting them trigger actions. Compare later against matured outcomes. Keep the original evidence frozen so hindsight cannot quietly rewrite the test.

I would rather see an honest comparison lose than a sophisticated aggregator win a contest designed around itself.

Open one trace before your next agent meeting

You can start without retraining anything. Pick one completed decision and ask:

  1. Can I recover every input, or only the winner?
  2. Does ‘confidence’ mean measured correctness, or just a vote fraction?
  3. Would identical ballots with different magnitudes or risks be distinguishable here?
  4. Can I tell a completed neutral decision from a refusal to decide?

One trace will not validate the whole system. It can reveal that you lack the records required to validate it at all. That is a useful discovery to make before the incident review.

The boundary around our result

This audit covers one five-year financial-research snapshot. The separately configured voices are not statistically independent samples. Dispersion and risk measures are model-derived, and the scoring policy itself helps determine the patterns observed.

The 45% is disagreement between methods across 365 decisive cases. It is not a failure rate across 4,523 judgments, a trading return, or evidence that either method outperformed the market.

What the audit does establish is that the ballot did not contain enough information to reproduce the richer decision. Whether those extra distinctions improve future outcomes remains an empirical question.

Back to those twelve green lights

Accenture. Adyen. The Trade Desk. Twelve STRONG BUY votes each. Two final rating levels. The puzzle disappears once you inspect what the labels left out.

That is the lesson I would carry into an agent-based code reviewer, approval workflow, or research assistant. Before celebrating agreement, ask what the application will never see.

The uncomfortable engineering question is not always ‘Which model should we add?’ Sometimes it is ‘Why did we pay for all this analysis and then keep only the label?’

Count the votes. Keep the evidence.

Then earn the right to act.

Which field would you most hate to discover missing from your agent logs after a bad decision?

Resources

  • Towards a science of scaling agent systems — Google Research
  • Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems — paper
  • Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation Using Deep Ensembles — NeurIPS
  • On the Foundations of Noise-free Selective Classification — JMLR
  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework
  • iPulse AI methodology — scoring definitions and research process

Research note

Source: an author-controlled July 2026 research snapshot covering 377 assets and 4,523 agent judgments at a five-year horizon. The analysis keeps the latest active version of each eligible asset/configuration, compares three-way vote winners with final model directions, and measures entropy across all five rating categories. Twelve tied votes are excluded from the 365-case disagreement denominator. Percentages are rounded. Reproduction SQL and analysis definitions are retained with the research package. This is an engineering case study, not personalized investment advice.

I Audited 4,523 AI Judgments. Here’s What I’d Check Before Trusting an Agent Team. was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
